Mapping the AI Supply Chain: Dependencies, Vulnerabilities, and Market Concentration in the AI Ecosystem

Sarah H. Cen Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University    Lindsey A. Gailmard Affiliation: Stanford University    Joohan Kim Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University    Rishi Bommasani Affiliation: Stanford University    Daniel E. Ho Affiliation: Stanford University    Percy Liang Affiliation: Stanford University
Abstract

AI systems are built across many organizations that contribute models, data, compute, capital, talent, and other assets. While the layers of the AI stack are relatively well understood, the relationships between actors and components across layers remains sparsely documented. In this work, we focus on the organizations that make up the AI supply chain: the complex network of actors that contribute to the development and deployment of AI. We motivate the examination of the organizational AI supply chain—highlighting concerns about concentration, power, chokepoints, cascading failures, fragmented accountability, and risk—then describe our pipeline for mapping the AI supply chain. Our pipeline yields our main contribution: a multilayered, large-scale dataset of actors and relationships in the AI ecosystem, annotated with dates, descriptions, types, tags, and more. This work takes a step toward systematially mapping and measuring the AI supply chain and its properties, cataloging how models, data, chips, infrastructure, capital, and even talent flow between organizations. This data enable critical examinations of industry relationships and yield insights into the political economy of AI development and concentration. We provide several illustrative analyses, including studying the most central actors, analyzing network concentration, and identifying communities and chokepoints. While our dataset is fairly comprehensive, it is also necessarily incomplete: public documents omit private deals, and coverage is shaped by search design. Together, the approach, data, and findings aim to serve as a resource for studying the AI ecosystem. The dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/sarahcen/ai-supply-chain and can be explored interactively at https://aisupplychains.org/.

1 Introduction

The production of AI-enabled technologies has become increasingly distributed across a diverse set of organizations. Rather than building end-to-end systems entirely in-house, firms now assemble AI capabilities from multiple sources, including model developers, data companies, and cloud infrastructure providers. These actors, in turn, rely on contributions from upstream actors, like semiconductor manufacturers and human data workers (Gray and Suri 2019; Miceli and Posada 2022). While we have a growing understanding of the AI stack (the layers of AI development and deployment), we lack a comparable understanding of the links between actors. We have little knowledge of how models, data, compute, capital, and talent flow between actors, as well as the competitive, regulatory, and political relationships in the AI industry.

Central to that conversation is the AI supply chain: the network of actors and components that contribute to AI development and deployment (Cobbe et al. 2023; Cen et al. 2023; Hopkins et al. 2025a). Although the AI “supply chain” can refer to a network of AI assets (e.g., with models or datasets as nodes), we focus on the organizational supply chain in this work. We define the organizational AI supply chain as a network of organizations connected in a graph by relationships relevant to AI development or deployment, where edges capture directional links. We say that an actor is upstream from another if it provides inputs that materially enable the latter’s AI-related activities. An actor that receives them is downstream. Under this definition, the AI supply chain spans contributors as far upstream as human annotators and hardware manufacturers, and as far downstream as the end-users of AI-enabled products. Actors may occupy different roles across relationships (e.g., upstream in some relationships and downstream in others) and feedback loops (e.g., user data to improve upstream models) are common. Some links are symmetric—such as partnerships and competition—manifesting as undirected edges. As a result, the structure is better understood as a network than as a linear chain or tree.

Focusing on organizational relationships captures consolidated and established power dynamics. Political economy scholarship has long emphasized that supply chains are not neutral conduits of production, but structures where power and governance are negotiated (Gereffi et al. 2005; Baldwin 2012). In traditional manufacturing networks, the structure of the supply-chain shapes downstream outcomes, including vulnerability to shocks, bargaining power between firms, and the feasibility of regulation. Similar dynamics are emerging in AI, with recent concerns arising around the ability of general-purpose AI technologies to impact a diverse array of sectors and applications and, as a result, risks. Because AI development relies on resources, like compute, data, and technical talent, that are themselves highly concentrated and geopolitically contested (Muldoon et al. 2025; Luitse and Denkena 2021; Widder et al. 2024), actors at the top of the AI supply chain who maintain control over resources are in a position to set prices and indirectly control downstream risks (Vipra and Korinek 2023; Korinek and Vipra 2025). Coordination and dealing-making at the top of the supply chain fuel worries that dominant AI actors are creating “kingmakers” (Gurun et al. 2025), fueling an unsustainable “AI bubble” (Caballero 2026; Floridi 2024), and neutralizing policymakers through regulatory capture (Wei et al. 2024). At the same time, there are concerns about vulnerabilities in the AI supply chain arising from chokepoints that create strong dependencies on specific nodes and, correspondingly, increase the risk of cascading failures. Alongside these concerns are issues of accountability (Widder and Nafus 2023), including questions about where responsibility for AI harms and risk management falls in the organizational AI supply chain.

Fundamentally, these issues can be traced to the simultaneous concentration of resources and control at the top of the supply chain, and a rapid expansion of downstream use and risk at the bottom. While these reflect different substantive concerns, evaluating them requires information not only about individual firms or components of the AI stack, but also about the relationships between organizations in the AI supply chain. Understanding and tackling such issues requires a systematic examination of the links, dependencies, and relationships between AI actors and not merely the AI stack. Despite its importance, the organizational AI supply chain remains poorly documented in a systematic way. Recent work has proposed conceptual frameworks and provided case studies highlighting the importance of supply chains for accountability (Cobbe et al. 2023), as well as empirical mappings of particular platforms (Laufer et al. 2025) or model families (Bommasani et al. 2023; van der Vlist et al. 2024).

In this paper, we build a pipeline for mapping the AI supply chain. Motivated by the fact that much of the AI supply chain emerged from the development of large language models (LLMs), we seed the mapping with 36 foundation model providers. The pipeline then performs a systematic online search, followed by an automated extraction and annotation of relationships contained in the resulting documents. The result is a dynamic, regularly updated network of relationships derived from public documents, such as news articles, press releases, company blogs, and online reports. We classify and analyze the structure of these relationships by developing a taxonomy of relationship types and use network analyses to study patterns, dependencies, and chokepoints, among other characteristics. In the process, we curate a dataset of over 13,000 documents dating from November 2022 to October 2026, resulting in a network of relationships between about 9,700 unique actors (4,520 when more aggressively filtering out infrequent actors). This dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/sarahcen/ai-supply-chain and can be explored interactively at https://aisupplychains.org/.

To illustrate the information contained in this dataset, we provide several quantitative and qualitative analyses. The data can be viewed as a multilayered network graph across time, with organizations as nodes and relationships as edges, where nodes and edges are further tagged and annotated. Accordingly, we provide several quantitative and qualitative analyses of the network, with illustrative examples of the relationships found in the data. In particular, we (1) examine the most central actors in the AI supply chain; (2) analyze network concentration; (3) identify communities and chokepoints in the network; (4) demonstrate how the data reveals close and even cyclical relationships; and (5) study how relationship narratives change across documents and evolve across time. We note that our analysis does not provide full coverage of the AI supply chain. Due to how the search is seeded, coverage is most complete and dense around large model providers. We discuss issues of coverage and limitations of our dataset in Section 4.4.

Our dataset and analysis shift attention from layers of the AI stack to the relationships that connect them. They provide a framework for identifying dependencies and potential chokepoints, while also demonstrating the limitations of relying on fragmented public disclosure to understand them. We hope that this dataset can serve as a useful resource that informs research, policymaking, and our broader understanding of the AI industry. We further aim to expand the dataset to improve coverage across relationships and actors.

2 The Organizational AI Supply Chain

In this work, the AI supply chain is understood as a network of organizations involved in the development and deployment of AI products, services, and other AI assets. This section describes the organizational AI supply chain, discussing the actors that exist within it and enumerating links between AI actors that have become salient in discussions of power, risk, resilience, and governance. Although individual people are key parts of the AI supply chain, our work takes organizations as its primary unit of analysis.

2.1 Organizational supply chain network

We represent the organizational AI supply chain as a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), where VV is the set of organizations (nodes) and EE is the set of links (edges) among them. That is, each v∈Vv\in V is an organization in the AI industry, and (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E indicates that there is a link between nodes uu and vv.

When a link is asymmetric, we treat an edge (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E as a directed edge from uu to vv. Such directed edges originate from an upstream actor who generally provides assets (such as models, compute, data, or chips) to a downstream actor. Many important AI relationships are directional in this sense and capture dependencies in the AI industry. These dependencies are precisely what allows the AI industry to become more efficient and specialized, but it also creates opportunities for chokepoints, bottlenecks, and vulnerabilities where a small number of actors can control the flow of assets, resources, or knowledge. Other links are symmetric, encoding explicit relationships (such as partnerships or agreements) and implicit ones (such as competition). When a relationship between actors uu and vv is symmetric, both (u,v)(u,v) and (v,u)(v,u) exist in EE.

Importantly, the AI supply chain consists of not only suppliers, but also users. Generally, upstream organizations are providers who possess significant sway because their behaviors impact all their descendants (all nodes that fall on a directed path originating from this organization, including its immediate downstream nodes and nodes that indirectly descend from it all the way down to the end-users). What counts as “upstream” or “downstream” is therefore relative to where in the AI supply chain one is focused: upstream means closer to the origin of a path, whereas downstream means closer to the end of the path.

Yet, not all links have a clear upstream or downstream organization. Specfically, when there is a cycle—a closed loop such that following a path from node uu leads back to uu—there is no clear notion of upstream or downstream. In the AI supply chain, cycles are significant because they indicate feedback loops. While some cycles signal that the AI industry is healthy and self-sustaining, others may indicate market concentration and anti-competitive behavior, such as circular financing (e.g., company A invests in company B, which invests in company C, which invests in company A) to inflate market value (Tierno 2026; Solanki 2026).

Finally, it is often helpful to take slices of GG or extract subnetworks from it. For instance, we may be interested in how the network evolves over time and split GG into a series of snapshots G1,G2,…,GTG_{1},G_{2},...,G_{T}. Alternatively, we may be interested in a specific type of relationship, such as model-related dependencies or the flow of capital, and analyze a subgraph of GG (e.g., the model supply chain or data supply chain), or even study the connections between different subgraphs (e.g., how model and data supply chains interact).

2.2 Nodes are organizational actors

In the organizational AI supply chain, an actor is an organization that participates in AI-related production, deployment, and deployment. In general, actors may take on more than one role in the AI industry; OpenAI serves as a research lab, a model provider, and chatbot deployer, for instance.

Illustrative roles along the organizational AI supply chain include the following. Far upstream, semiconductor designers and manufacturers (e.g., NVIDIA, AMD, TSMC, ASML) provide chips. Cloud and compute providers (e.g., Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud) sit between hardware and model developers, offering training and inference capacity. Data providers and annotators (e.g., Scale AI, Mercor) source and supply data for model training and customization. Foundation and base model providers (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta AI, Mistral) provide large models and APIs that downstream firms adapt and consume. Surrounding them are firms that provide tooling, infrastructure, and evaluations. Further downstream are other model providers, application builders, enterprise users, and consumers. Capital actors (e.g., venture firms) finance and take ownership stakes in AI firms. Universities, national labs, and independent research institutes develop their own models, datasets, and methods alongisde industry actors, often partnering with them (Ahmed et al. 2023). Public bodies (e.g., NIST, FTC, state governments) support, regulate, and procure AI. Other roles include standards setting bodies, civil society organizations, and AI safety non-profits.

Importantly, actors frequently occupy several roles at once (e.g., a cloud provider that also trains models and distributes applications). As mentioned before, an actor may therefore be “upstream” of one organization and “downstream” of another.

2.3 Edges are links, relationships, and dependencies

Actors alone do not constitute a supply chain. What forms the AI supply chain are the links between actors. For instance, one of the most common relationships is a provision: one actor supplies goods, services, access, or capabilities to another. These relationships are useful for identifying potential chokepoints in AI production. Investment and financing relationships concern how capital flows, introducing financial dependencies and potential conflicts of interest. Ownership and control relationships capture acquisitions, subsidiaries, and other analogous arrangements. In our data, partnerships and collaborations are highly common and include coordinated efforts and alliances between organizations. Many remaining relationships concern employment and personnel, regulation and oversight, and even competition.

The ways in which actors are connected influence power, risk, resilience, and governance in the AI industry. These links are central to our analysis; as we describe in the following sections, isolating particular types of relationships, links, and dependencies lets us study slices of the multilayered AI supply chain.

2.4 Why the organizational supply chain matters

The organizational supply chain arises organically because specialization improves efficiency. That is, rather than have a single organization perform every operation in AI development, different organizations specialize in specific processes or components of AI. This specialization allows them to develop context-specific practices and improve overall efficiency. However, specialization can also create interdependence that affects the distribution of power and transmission of shocks. We briefly name several implications of supply chain characteristics that motivate our analysis of the organizational structure of the AI ecosystem.

  1. 1.

    Dependencies create power. Dependencies show who relies on whom for scarce inputs such as compute, data, and model access. Mapping these ties surfaces structures of power in the AI industry.

  2. 2.

    The supply chain network reveals areas of market concentration. An organizational map shows where concentration of resources such as capital, compute, and data sits. Market concentration can be concerning because a few actors can set terms of access, limit entry, and shape competition across layers of the AI ecosystem.

  3. 3.

    Bottlenecks and chokepoints create vulnerabilities and cascading failures. When certain flows of AI assets are controlled by a small number of actors, bottlenecks and chokepoints arise. Such structures can amplify local shocks, making them system-wide.

  4. 4.

    The supply chain illustrates where risk arises and propagates. Where AI risk arises is one of the main concerns of the AI industry. An organizational map can illustrate not only where risk originates, but also where it may be inherited or propagated across organizations, their behaviors, and their offerings.

  5. 5.

    The supply chain complicates liability and responsibility, but mapping it can help. When many organizations jointly produce and deploy AI systems, responsibility and liability becomes fragmented. Mapping the links between organizations is a necessary step to improving accountability, e.g., by clarifying where along the chain regulatory intervention is most likely to be effective.

3 Mapping the Organizational AI Supply Chain: Methodology

In this section, we describe the procedure for tracking and extracting relationships in the organizational AI supply chain. Our pipeline is fully automated and runs regularly, with extensive error handling and retry logic, to create an up-to-date archive of AI supply chain relationships. We use publicly available information, including news articles, press releases, and company blogs. Our pipeline collects these documents from November 2022 until the present via targeted Google Search queries over one-month time windows. For each seed organization, query, and time window, we collect Google Search results via SerpAPI. We then scrape the linked pages when accessible, extracting title and body text. Scraped documents are processed using an LLM that identifies relationships described in the document and taxonomizes the relationships and actors involved. The relationship data is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/sarahcen/ai-supply-chain and can be explored at https://aisupplychains.org/.

3.1 Data sources

We rely on public data sources. We intentionally use publicly available documents rather than paywalled APIs or other proprietary data to allow for reproducibility, verifiability, and traceability of all results. That is, all users should be able to examine the original text that gave rise to any relationships in our dataset. We thus do not use datasets, such as Bloomberg Terminal or PitchBook. Table 7 lists the most common source domains among successfully scraped pages. Common domains include finance.yahoo.com, techcrunch.com, linkedin.com, venturebeat.com, huggingface.co, cnbc.com, and medium.com.

To assemble a broad corpus of publicly accessible documents, we use Google Search. Our searches primarily surface news articles, press releases, and company blogs. The dataset includes product launches, strategic partnerships, funding announcements, and litigation, among other events and decisions. Generally, each reported event or decision is covered by more than one document, introducing helfpul redundancies in the data. For instance, press releases and marketing materials may emphasize positive narratives and gloss over risks or other issues, while news reporting and blogs may provide countervailing perspectives.

3.2 Search pipeline

The first stage of our pipeline is a search pipeline that uses SerpAPI to run targeted Google Search queries over one-month periods from November 2022 until the present. We seed the search pipeline with a list of starting AI organizations. In deciding how to seed the search, we chose to use large general-purpose or foundation model providers. This choice reflects prior analyses of the AI supply chain in that its emergence was facilitated by general-purpose or foundation models that lowered the barrier to entry to AI development and deployment and thus catalyzed broad AI adoption. Based on this thesis, this work begins with 36 major model providers: 01.ai, AI2, AI21 Labs, Adept, Aleph Alpha, Alibaba, Amazon, Anthropic, Baidu, Bytedance, Cartesia, Cohere, Contextual AI, Databricks, DeepMind, DeepSeek, EleutherAI, Google AI, Huawei, Hugging Face, IBM AI, Inflection, Krutrim, LightOn, Meta AI, Microsoft AI, Midjourney, Mistral AI, NVIDIA, Numenta, OpenAI, Reka, Snowflake, Stability AI, Together AI, xAI.

This choice of seed organizations introduces some coverage bias, as we discuss in Section 3.6. We note that our AI supply chain dataset is not limited to just these seed organizations. Through our search pipeline, we recover a much wider set of organizations (about 9,700 after fuzzy and common-sense deduplication, and about 4,500 after dropping actors that appear in fewer than three rows of our dataset; see Section 4). Thus, this list helps initiate a search that includes a broader umbrella of organizations, though it is of course not exhaustive.

Finally, we note that our pipeline can be easily adapted to include more seed organizations—it would only require changing the search configuration. Because our pipeline first locates the most recent search for an organization, it would find that there is no recent search for a new organization and therefore initiate a new search dating back to November 2022.

For each seed organization, we run a series of SerpAPI Google Search queries. Specifically, we run (i) one broad query of the form "OrgName" <keyword string> and (ii) three site-restricted queries "OrgName" <keyword string> site:<domain>. The <keyword string> values we use are

  1. 1.

    (partnership OR collaboration OR agreement OR alliance)

  2. 2.

    (deal OR investment OR acquisition OR merger OR licensing)

The site:<domain> values we use are techcrunch.com, venturebeat.com, and finance.yahoo.com—these sites supplement the broad search, they do not replace it. (As mentioned above, other keyword strings and sites can be easily added.) Thus each search is determined by a combination of organization, query type, keyword string, and site domain for site-specific searches.

For each combination of queries, we further split the time period of our search into one-month intervals to ensure good coverage across time (otherwise, the Google Search ranking algorithm would favor the most popular and recent results). Specifically, since we collect results from November 2022 onwards, we split the time period from the start date until the present into one-month windows, then run each of the queries described above. We collect up to 15 results per broad query and up to 5 results per site-restricted query per one-month period. The search pipeline is updated regularly, using the last successful search date as the start date for the new search. There is expected variation in search results by location; we use San Francisco as our location. Although providing multiple locations could help, due to the volume of search queries, we limited our search to a single location.

The fields of the search results table are given in Table 8.

3.3 Scraping pipeline

After search results are collected, the second stage of the pipeline scrapes the content of each unique document link. This stage regularly looks for any unscraped links in the output of the search pipeline, then runs page scraping with up to 3 retries. It uses a headless Chrome browser (via undetected Chromedriver). It first looks for content in <main> or <article> when present, falling back to a heuristic that scans every div, section, and article for the container with the greatest number of non-empty <p> tags. The stored fields include the URL, title, document date, and snippet (which are metadata from the search pipeline) as well as body text and date of scrape (which are from the scraping pipeline).

Failures are tracked and retried up to 3 times. Failures are generally due to sites being paywalled, being blocked by bot detection, and requiring logins to access content. Only non-empty scrapes are kept. The fields of the scraping results table are given in Table 9.

3.4 LLM post-processing

The final stages of the pipeline run a series of post-processing steps to taxonomize the data. To do so, we use a series of calls to gpt-5.6-luna with strict structured outputs, medium reasoning, and medium verbosity. We run two independent extraction passes per document.

Site and document classification. After a page is scraped, it is assigned a site type (based primarily on the domain name) and a document type (based on URL, title, and snippet). The allowed site and document types are given in Table 9.

Relationship extraction. From each scraped page, the LLM extracts pairwise relationships using the page text and title. A document may yield zero, one, or many relationships. Long documents are split into chunks of about 150,000 tokens. We run two independent passes per document. For each relationship, the model returns the two actor names, a one-sentence description of the relationship, a short description of the evidence for the relationship, a label indicating the strength of the evidence, and an AI-relevance label. The actor names follow how they appear in the source text. Thus, while clear variants within a document may be normalized, the same actor may be encoded under different names in the database. This design is intentional, as it allows the relationships to closely mirror the source text; one can then de-duplicate actor names using a desired post-processing procedure.

Actor classification. In the next step, each actor is assigned one actor type. The allowable actor types are: COMPANY; NONPROFIT_OR_CIVIL_SOCIETY; ACADEMIC_INSTITUTION; COALITION_OR_CONSORTIUM; PERSON; GOVERNMENT_BODY; GEOPOLITICAL_ENTITY_OR_COUNTRY; INTERGOVERNMENTAL_OR_SUPRANATIONAL; OTHER_ACTOR; NOT_AN_ACTOR; UNKNOWN_OR_UNCLEAR.

Relationship classification. Further, each relationship is also assigned a relationship type, a relationship status, up to two AI stack layers, a directionality label, and (when AI-related) up to three AI topics. The released Hugging Face repo only contains relationships for which the AI relevance label is either AI_RELATIONSHIP or INVOLVES_AI_ACTOR, dropping relationships labeled NOT_AI_RELATED or UNCLEAR. The allowable relationship types are: INVESTMENT; PROVISION; OWNERSHIP; EVALUATION; PARTNERSHIP; ONE_SIDED_DEPENDENCY; EMPLOYMENT; AFFILIATION; REGULATION; INFLUENCE; COMPETITION; DISPUTE; INCIDENT; PUBLIC_STATEMENT; NO_RELATIONSHIP; OTHER; and UNCLEAR. The allowable relationship statuses are ESTABLISHED, PROPOSED, ENDED, NOT_APPLICABLE, and UNCLEAR. The allowable AI stack layers (one or two per relationship) are: CAPITAL; HARDWARE; INFRASTRUCTURE; DATA; RESEARCH; MODELS; PLATFORMS; APPLICATIONS; ADOPTION; OPERATIONS; SAFETY; SECURITY; GOVERNANCE; TALENT; and, alone, NOT_AI_STACK or UNKNOWN_OR_UNCLEAR. The allowable AI relationship categories are the 117 AI tags in the AI-tag taxonomy; examples include AI_COMPUTE; AI_SEMICONDUCTORS; AI_MODELS; AI_SOFTWARE; AI_DATA; AI_APPLICATIONS; AI_RESEARCH; AI_TALENT; AI_FUNDING; AI_OWNERSHIP; AI_PARTNERSHIP; AI_MARKET_ACCESS; AI_REGULATION; AI_POLICY; AI_GOVERNANCE; AI_SAFETY; AI_HARMS; AI_INTELLECTUAL_PROPERTY; AI_INFRASTRUCTURE; AI_ENERGY; AI_SECURITY; and AI_DEFENSE (the full list is in the dataset schema). Directionality is one of ACTOR_1_TO_ACTOR_2, ACTOR_2_TO_ACTOR_1, SYMMETRIC, or UNCLEAR. A directed label names the source and the target; it does not depend on which actor is listed first.

The full system and user prompts are included in Appendix A. These prompts clearly state the scope of each label.

3.5 The dataset

Each row in the public dataset (https://huggingface.co/datasets/sarahcen/ai-supply-chain) corresponds to a relationship extraction. Table 1 summarizes the fields that appear in the released dataset. Full details can be found in Table 16. Note that rows do not represent unique relationships for two reasons: (i) many documents may cover the same relationship, and (ii) our pipeline runs relationship extraction twice per document.

3.6 Limitations

Our dataset has several notable limitations. First, because we choose to use publicly available documents, we forego several high-quality data sources that are available (such as Bloomberg Terminal and PitchBook). Second, our data comes from Google Search. Thus, our results are affected by Google’s search algorithm (e.g., high-quality but low-traffic sources may be missed) and what sites are search indexed. Third, our search and LLM processing is in English, meaning that the results and documents we use are primarily English-language sources. Fourth, there may be confidential or proprietary information on links, dependencies, or relationships that we are unable to observe from public data.

Our search is also affected by design choices that we made around (i) the list of seed organizations, (ii) our choice of keywords strings, (iii) our choice of sites to supplement the broad search, (iv) the search location being San Francisco, CA. These choices were informed by significant testing, but we faced trade-offs between coverage on one end and cost and redundancy on the other. Of these, the choice of seed organizations is likely the most significant. As noted above, we can and hope to expand the seed organization list in the future. At the moment, it is biased toward the portion of the supply chain closest to large model providers. Ultimately, there is coverage bias, but the organizational AI supply chain that this pipeline surfaces yields meaningful insights; wherever coverage bias may affect our results and discussion, we do our best to disclose this limitation. We provide statistics on our dataset in Sections 4 and C.

In our scraping stage, the main limitation is that scraping is not possible when there are paywalled sites or bot detection mechanisms. In our LLM processing stage, the main limitations are around (i) our choice of taxonomy, and (ii) the LLM’s accuracy and hallucination rates. LLMs always have false positive and false negative rates, where false positives (hallucinations) are most concerning. In our analysis, we do our best to avoid these by dropping actors that appear in fewer than three relationships after name normalization (and, in some figures, by requiring repeated documentary support for an edge). However, critical edges should always be checked against the linked source. As a verification, we randomly sampled 50 relationships and manually checked the article title, both actor names, the relationship type, and the relationship status against the linked source. Forty-five were verified on all five fields. Of the remaining five, four sources could not be checked (e.g., due to pages no longer existing), and one relationship had correct information but an incorrect relationship status (PROPOSED instead of ESTABLISHED). See Section A.6 for details.

There are two final limitations. First, the documents themselves may be biased. For instance, press releases can overstate, omit, or misrepresent relationships. Second, because there is no canonical notion of what an “organization” is, it is impossible to fully deduplicate our data. For instance, there is ambiguity in whether Google DeepMind should be collapsed under Google or, further, Alphabet. For some users, they may wish to distinguish between, e.g., Google DeepMind and Google Cloud; for other users, they may wish to collapse them all under Google. In our analysis, we do our best to clarify how we handle this ambiguity.

4 Exploring the Dataset

The main contribution of this work is the dataset. One can think of this dataset as a multilayered adjacency matrix, where each edge is annotated with a natural language description, multiple categorical labels (e.g., relationship type, actor type, AI tag), source document, document date, and more (as described in Section 3). This adjacency matrix allows one to explore the organizational AI supply chain across time and by category, using longstanding graph analysis techniques as well. To explore the capacity of this dataset, this section provides illustrative examples of information contained within it.

For the remainder of our analysis, we show results for a filtered graph G′G^{\prime}, unless otherwise stated. To obtain this filtered graph, we keep only rows with document_date from November 1, 2022 through the end of October 2026 that are AI-related (AI_RELATIONSHIP or INVOLVES_AI_ACTOR). We then exclude rows that have null dates; actors with types PERSON, NOT_AN_ACTOR, or UNKNOWN_OR_UNCLEAR; relationship type COMPETITION, PUBLIC_STATEMENT, NO_RELATIONSHIP, UNCLEAR, or CONTRADICTORY_INFORMATION; directionality UNCLEAR or CONTRADICTORY_INFORMATION; relationship status ENDED, NOT_APPLICABLE, UNCLEAR, or CONTRADICTORY_INFORMATION; or AI stack layers with NOT_AI_STACK or UNKNOWN_OR_UNCLEAR. We further deduplicate actor names using fuzzy actor matching and common-sense groupings (such as mapping DeepMind, Alphabet, and Gemini to Google). We drop actors that appear in fewer than three rows across the corpus and keep an edge only if both endpoints meet that threshold. We further normalize edges by collapsing all relationships that, within a given month, share the same actor pair, directionality, and relationship type.11 1 As mentioned in Section 3, we do not filter the publicly released data. We intentionally allow the data to closely reflect the information in the source documents, as different users of the dataset may wish to filter and deduplicate in their own ways.

The resulting G′G^{\prime} has 4,520 actors and 37,472 edges (from 100,079 relationships and 15,406 raw actor strings that arise with no filtering).

4.3 Complex directed network

While one can extract subtrees from the dataset, the underlying network is much more complex. To illustrate this point, consider Figure 4. Although we are unable to render the entire graph, as it is too large, this figure shows a small slice focused on established capital and investment relationships in the first half of 2026, pruning to the top 24 actors by weighted degree and their one-hop neighbors (the graph includes INVESTMENT edges with stack label CAPITAL and exclude relationships with endpoints PERSON, direction SYMMETRIC, in addition to the filter applied to G′G^{\prime}). We emphasize that this by no means a complete graph; it is an illustrative slice obtained by filtering the graph, taking a snapshot of January to June 2026, then further pruning.

While they emerge from the same dataset, this graph provides a more holistic view than the subtrees, demonstrating that some edges are bidirectional and that the graph contains cycles. In this graph that focuses on relationships involving capital, Anthropic, NVIDIA, and OpenAI are the highest-degree hubs, and Mistral AI, xAI, Microsoft, Cohere, Contextual AI, Reka AI, and Amazon also rank among the top ten. Other hubs include Google, Snowflake, Lightspeed, Together AI, Andreessen Horowitz, Sequoia Capital, Hugging Face, Radical Ventures, 01.AI, Salesforce, Alibaba, DST Global, Coatue, and Runway.

4.4 Coverage and composition

The organizational AI supply chain in this work is extracted from public documents. This approach introduces coverage bias in multiple ways: not all activities are publicly reported; some events and links are reported multiple times while others are reported only once; and the same event or link may be described in different ways. In this section, we briefly examine the coverage of this dataset. More extensive statistics are provided in the Appendix. We also explore how coverage of the same event or link varies in Section 5.5.

We begin with Figure 5, which shows the composition of relationship types, actor types, and AI tags. It shows the count of the ten most common categories in each bar plot, according to the filtered graph G′G^{\prime}. This figure shows that the dataset consists primarily of partnerships, provisions, and investments, followed by one-sided dependencies. Further, companies are by far the most well represented actor type. Within AI-specific tags, the relationships span diverse activities and assets, including partnerships, investments, software, applications, models, and infrastructure.

Although these histograms illustrate the composition of the dataset, they may simply reflect the composition of the AI industry rather than biases in the dataset. To further examine where the dataset may contain coverage bias, we use the month collapse already built into G′G^{\prime}. Relationships that have the same endpoints, type, directionality, and month are collapsed into a single relationship. Of these, about 8.3% are in three or more documents, about 11.6% are in two documents, and about 80.1% are in one. There is a long tail where 35 documents share the same endpoints, type, directionality, and month. Figure 6 show where redundancy occurs, by relationship in (a) and by seed organization in (b). By Figure 6(a), incident, ownership, and investment relationship types have the highest mean documents per collapsed edge, followed by employment, dispute, regulation, partnership, and provision. Although the means seem low (close to 1), that is because most ties are mentioned in a single document, and there is a long right tail. Further, certain organizations often receive repeat coverage. In Figure 6(b), we plot the maximum number of documents cover the same relationship (according to the month collapse described above) that involves each seed organization for 12 seed organizations. As seen, coverage of OpenAI, Microsoft, Hugging Face, NVIDIA, and xAI, among others, can be redundant within our dataset. Further statistics are provided in Appendix F. 5 Five Analyses of the Dataset

In this section, we conduct five analyses using the dataset. Although the dataset is our main contribution, our findings demonstrate how the dataset can be used to answer questions about the AI industry.

5.1 Analysis #1: Actors with the largest impact on the AI supply chain

To isolate the top actors across the organizational AI supply chain, we use multiple metrics and “layers” of the supply chain, as shown in Table 2. The table lists the top 15 actors by total degree on two filtered subgraphs of G′G^{\prime}. In addition to the filters applied to obtain G′G^{\prime}, this table requires relationship statuses to be ESTABLISHED. Table 2(a) excludes AI stack layers TALENT and relationship types REGULATION, INFLUENCE, DISPUTE, INCIDENT, (so it keeps PROVISION, INVESTMENT, OWNERSHIP, PARTNERSHIP, EMPLOYMENT, AFFILIATION, EVALUATION, and ONE_SIDED_DEPENDENCY). Panel (b) keeps PROVISION only and excludes AI stack layers CAPITAL, RESEARCH, GOVERNANCE, TALENT, NOT_AI_STACK, and UNKNOWN_OR_UNCLEAR. Table 2 further restricts to relationship type PROVISION.

As shown, during the period from November 2022 to October 2026, the top actors are Google, NVIDIA, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic. The ordering, however, varies depending on the metric of choice. Based on the overall rankings in Table 2(a), Google tops the list by degree and betweenness centrality, OpenAI by PageRank, and NVIDIA by the number of two-hop descendants. Further, when restricted to provisions only, DeepSeek and Together AI displace xAI and Alibaba in the top 15.

The differences between rankings across metrics point to different ways of thinking about supply chain “impact”. While the high degree and betweenness centrality imply that a node is highly connected, high PageRank indicates that a node is well positioned relative to other influential nodes, and the number of two-hop descendants suggests that a node is influential based on its downstream influence.

The order of organizations under degree, PageRank, and betweenness centrality is significantly different from that given by the number of two-hop descendants. This difference suggests that one should more closely consider directionality in a supply chain. To do so, we use SpringRank, a hierarchy score indicating how much “upstream” influence an actor has and that is capable of handling cycles in a directed network (one can view it as a more systematic metric than number of two-hop descendants). For instance, if a directed network is simply a line, then the SpringRank is simply the order of those nodes.

Table 3 examines upstream-downstream rankings using SpringRank. It is applied on the same graph as Table 2(a)(a), except that only actors with total weighted degree at least 50 are included; (a) is PROVISION excluding AI stack layers CAPITAL, RESEARCH, GOVERNANCE, and TALENT. Panel (b) uses those same edges, restricted to edges whose AI stack layers include MODELS. A higher score indicates a node is more upstream.

Under this new metric, the list shifts dramatically. The highest SpringRank scores in (a) are held by chip and infrastructure suppliers—TSMC, Groq, Crusoe, GMI Cloud, IREN, and Broadcom. Lower on the supply chain are government and enterprise buyers (United States, India, U.S. federal agencies, U.S. military, Uber, and Salesforce). Restricting further to edges whose stack layers include MODELS, the upstream list shifts to Together AI, Amazon, NVIDIA, Cohere, Alibaba, and Anthropic. Downstream are U.S. military and federal agencies, along with Apple, Snowflake, Hugging Face, and IBM.

As we note throughout this work, our supply chain is incomplete; it is constructed by scraping public data sources based on a search seeded with foundation or large model providers. Therefore, all rankings and numbers in this section are skewed accordingly.

Takeaway: A small set of actors—including Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, NVIDIA, and Anthropic—dominate centrality rankings. Using SpringRank to identify who is upstream and downstream reveals that chip and infrastructure suppliers lie further up the chain, while government and many enterprise buyers sit further down. When restricted to model provision s, model and cloud suppliers are more upstream.

5.2 Analysis #2: Concentration in the organizational AI supply chain

Zooming out, a major concern in the AI industry is market concentration. To better understand this topic, we compute several metrics—Num Nodes, the Gini coefficient, the top 10% share, and the Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI)—across different slices of the network, as shown in Tables 4 and 7.

To compute Table 4, we start from G′G^{\prime} over November 2022 through October 2026 and further restrict to company-company established ties (excluding relationship types PUBLIC_STATEMENT, INCIDENT, DISPUTE, COMPETITION, and REGULATION). We then slice that overall graph as indicated in the “Slice” column of Table 4 (compute/hardware correspond to AI tags AI_SEMICONDUCTORS, AI_COMPUTE, and AI_HARDWARE; data to AI_DATA, AI_DATA_ANNOTATION, and AI_SYNTHETIC_DATA; and models to AI_MODELS, AI_MODEL_TRAINING, and AI_MODEL_ADAPTATION). Figure 7 uses the same overall filter on three-month bins from December 2022 through June 2026. Num Nodes is the actor count in a given slice, the Gini coefficient captures the inequality of nodes’ market “share” within the slice (0 when every actor has the same strength and 1 when one actor holds all of it), the top 10% share is the fraction of total number of month-based relationships held by the strongest 10% of actors, and the HHI is the sum of squared market “shares” where market share is computed as the fraction of month-based relationships held by a node to the total number of relationships (where 11 indicates a monopoly and 1/Num​Nodes1/\mathrm{Num\ Nodes} indicates equality). The reciprocal 1/HHI1/\mathrm{HHI} gives the number of actors who, if they possessed equal market share, would produce the same HHI score. A large value indicates that the distribution is more equal in that each possesses very small market share and a value of 11 indicates unequal market share because 11 actor holds all of it. (Note that this metric is not normalized. One should compare it to Num Nodes in the network slice, but we leave it unnormalized because 1/HHI1/\mathrm{HHI} provides an interpretable value).

The metrics in Table 4 show that the network is fairly concentrated, with an overall Gini of 0.835 and the lowest slice Gini on AI data at 0.764. The top 10% of actors control about 80.0% of relationship strength overall. The overall HHI is 0.020, which implies that two randomly drawn relationships involve the same actor about 2.0% of the timen, which is approximately 72 times the 0.027% rate one would expect if all actors were equal. Note that HHI is normally used to determine market concentration, where edges correspond to market strength. In our work, edge weight tracks the number of relationships rather than market strength: if nodes were instead weighted by, for example, revenue-based market share, the measured concentration would likely be higher.

The highest HHI is held by the AI compute/hardware slice, at 0.054, followed by AI models at 0.036. To better interpret HHI, its reciprocal 1/HHI1/\mathrm{HHI} indicates how many equal actors would produce the same metric; one can then compare that number to Num Nodes in the slice for a sense of the skew. For AI models, 1/HHI1/\mathrm{HHI} is about 27.6. Given that our pipeline is seeded with 36 model providers and the network therefore has the most complete coverage across model providers, that 1/HHI1/\mathrm{HHI} is lower than 36 indicates (i) that the model supply chain is fairly concentrated, especially given that the slice has 1,204 nodes; and (ii) that our coverage is fairly good, whereas a higher 1/HHI1/\mathrm{HHI} than 36 would be a sign of incomplete coverage.

Figure 7 shows these metrics on the overall filtered graph from December 2022 to June 2026 in three-month bins. In Figure 7(a), the number of nodes and edges per three-month period continues to rise steadily, rising most sharply from late 2024 into early 2025. Despite that increase, Figure 7(b) shows that concentration is also increasing. Although the Gini and the top 10% share fall between December 2022 and December 2023, all three metrics—the Gini, the top 10% share, and 1/HHI1/\mathrm{HHI}—trend roughly upward over time.

Takeaway: The organizational AI supply chain is highly concentrated across metrics, and most concentrated for compute/hardware and models. Concentration is rising across time even as the number of actors grows, suggesting that activity among the largest companies is increasing faster than the fringe expands.

5.3 Analysis #3: Identifying communities and chokepoints

Most supply chain networks are not balanced. Rather, they are made up of clusters. To determine these clusters, we run Louvain community detection—an algorithm that groups together actors that share many of the same neighbors—on the weighted but undirected G′G^{\prime}.

We find that the network is dominated by several overlapping communities. On the full network, Louvain modularity, which measures how distinct communities are, is 0.416, and about 55.4% of edges still cross between communities. The overall network has a significant amount of overlap between communities, but this overlap starts to break down when we look at individual slices of the network: for example, the investment and partnership slices have more distinct communities (modularity 0.549 and 0.481), which is consistent with clustering based on repeated interactions between the same investors and AI companies and between the same partners.

The largest communities follow familiar geopolitical and product lines (Table 5(a)). The largest includes Databricks, Together, ElevenLabs, Cartesia, and Y Combinator, alongside about 590 others. The second largest includes Google, Perplexity, Apple, and the Allen Institute for AI. The OpenAI-Microsoft bloc (with AMD, Oracle, and SoftBank) is the fourth largest. Further groups follow geographic lines—such as the DeepSeek, Alibaba, ByteDance, United States, and Huawei community—as well as product lines, such as the community with NVIDIA, Intel, Open Secure AI Alliance, Cisco, and Dell. Interestingly, many of the actors with the highest centrality scores in Table 2 fall into distinct communities. We note that these communities indicate repeated interaction between actors across the public documents in our dataset, but are not based on formal contracts.

Studying communities also allows us to ask: where are there chokepoints? Specifically, one of the main concerns in a supply chain are bottlenecks because they introduce fragility. For instance, if an actor’s product goes down or is compromised, the impact on the rest of the network depends on that actor’s influence. Although centrality and downstream influence are examined in Section 5.1, the cross-community degree—the number of neighbors that lie in a different Louvain component—is another way to assess influence. We report cross-community degree on overall G′G^{\prime} and on the AI compute/hardware, AI data, and AI models slices (Table 5(b)), using the same tag groupings as in Table 4 and re-running Louvain within each network slice. The rankings in Table 5(b) names are similar actors to Table 2, and the fact that similar organizations sit at the top of the cross-community degree rankings suggests that the same actors play multiple roles in the network. These actors are not only central, but they bridge communities, meaning that the network is sensitive to the failure of these actors. In particular, when communities correspond to the production of specific AI assets (such as chips), actors with high cross-community degree form the “connective tissue” of AI development.

Takeaway: The network contains overlapping communities that are split along geopolitical and product lines. A small number of organizations have both high centrality values (as per Table 2) and cross-community degree (as per Table 5(b)), meaning that they are not only well connected, but also serve as bridges across geopolitical and production-based communities.

5.4 Analysis #4: Close and cyclical relationships persist across time

This dataset also provides a record of relationships, across different data sources and across time. For example, one can easily identify persistent relationships, such as those included in Table 6. We say that a relationship is persistent if the same two actors are linked in many distinct months. As shown, Microsoft and OpenAI are linked in 48 months, with investment in all 48 and partnership in 47; provision recurs in 39. Anthropic and Google are linked in 44 months and likewise mix investment, provision, and partnership. To diversify beyond those four organizations, the next most persistent pairs that avoid them are Meta-NVIDIA, X-xAI, and Amazon-NVIDIA, which are provision-based rather than financing-based, and China-United States, whose persistence is driven by regulation.

The following relationships were obtained from G′G^{\prime} by running simple natural language queries over the adjacency matrix and a corresponding CSV of relationship descriptions. These examples highlight close and cyclical relationships that indicate how capital moves through the AI industry and the dynamics between AI organizations, as well as how dynamics in the AI industry can be easily extracted from the dataset. Each quotation below comes from our dataset’s relationship descriptions.

5.5 Analysis #5: Different documents portray relationships differently across time

The organizational AI supply chain that we construct in this work is extracted from public documents. One interesting consequence of doing so is that the same relationship, event, or link may be contained in multiple documents. Interestingly, this can introduce multiple narratives about the same relationship, which is both a form of bias in our dataset as well as a source of information. For example, 26 documents cover a relationship between OpenAI and Reddit between May 2024 and September 2026.

The relationship begins as a strategic partnership, with mutual benefits on both sides. Initial articles in May 2024 report that the two organizations have entered a strategic partnership. OpenAI is described as ‘‘gaining access to a wealth of diverse and up-to-date content, which could prove invaluable in the development and refinement of its AI models,’’ and Reddit as able to ‘‘bring its vision of an AI-enhanced user experience to life, potentially offering personalized content recommendations, advanced moderation tools, and other innovative features.’’5353 53 https://venturebeat.com/technology/openai-partners-with-reddit-to-integrate-unique-user-generated-content-into-chatgpt

Some analyses of data partnerships predict a closed data ecosystem with users left behind. A TechCrunch article in June 2024 argues that AI training data will become something that only big tech companies are able to access, and Kyle Lo states that ‘‘entities governing content that’s potentially useful for AI development are incentivized to lock up their materials.’’ The article adds that ‘‘users aren’t seeing a dime of the profits,’’ citing that data has become so valuable that multiple big tech companies are reportedly risking lawsuits to train or entering into expensive data licensing agreements like those with Reddit.5454 54 https://techcrunch.com/2024/06/01/ai-training-data-has-a-price-tag-that-only-big-tech-can-afford/

Reddit reinforces the message that people are still independently visiting Reddit and that the relationship with AI companies can be productive. In October 2025, a TechCrunch article reports that Reddit CEO Steve Huffman says that AI chatbots are ‘‘not a major traffic driver today.’’ Instead, Huffman says that most traffic to Reddit comes from search and direct access. At the same time, the article reports that Reddit has ‘‘locked down its data through a new policy change’’ and ‘‘indicated that any kind of commercial use of its data would need a license.’’5555 55 https://techcrunch.com/2025/10/31/reddit-ceo-says-chatbots-are-not-a-traffic-driver/

Reddit reports revenue from data licensing. In July 2025, TechCrunch reports that Reddit’s ‘‘other revenue’’ category, ‘‘which includes its data licensing business---meaning its deals with AI providers for access to its data,’’ ‘‘jumped 24% year-over-year to $35 million.’’5656 56 https://techcrunch.com/2025/07/31/reddit-revenue-soars-as-it-bets-on-ai-and-advertising/

Narrative changes as Reddit traffic drops. In July 2026, CNBC reports that Google AI summaries are reducing traffic to websites, so Reddit is reconsidering the benefits of deals with AI companies (in this particular article, a deal with Google). Even as Reddit stock falls 8%, Reddit CEO Huffman reiterated that partnerships with Google and OpenAI are ‘‘very meaningful’’ to them, and ‘‘I think it’s mutual.’’5757 57 https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/22/reddit-stock-google-ai-content-deal.html

The licensing relationship itself is framed as time-limited and uncertain. In September 2026, Yahoo Finance reports that Reddit’s ‘‘data licensing deals with … Google and OpenAI are set to expire next year, and Wall Street simply can’t decide whether these deals are a windfall or a warning sign.’’ It describes OpenAI’s agreement as ‘‘giving its products access to Reddit’s real-time content,’’ ‘‘estimated around $70 million’’ and ‘‘set to expire soon.’’5858 58 https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/reddit-next-ai-catalyst-isn-121429089.html

Takeaway: The dataset provides coverage across sources and time, illustrating how relationships are framed and evolve.

6 Related Work

Our work draws on three related strands of research: conceptual treatments of AI and algorithmic supply chains; empirical efforts to map AI ecosystems; and governance and accountability frameworks that address distributed responsibility in complex sociotechnical systems. We discuss the relevant literature in these domains and highlight that empirical documentation of the organizational relationships that constitute these supply chains is relatively underdeveloped.

6.1 AI and Algorithmic Supply Chains

Early conceptual treatments of algorithmic supply chains emerged in response to concerns about distributed responsibility. As AI systems become more complex and modular, responsibility of their development, deployment, and operation falls on many actors rather than a single organization (Cobbe et al. 2023). The distributed nature of production and maintenance gives rise to what scholars have labeled the “many hands” problem in algorithmic systems (Slota et al. 2023). This complicates traditional approaches to accountability, which often assume more centralized control.

Cobbe et al. (2023) propose the concept of an algorithmic supply chain to describe flows “where several actors contribute towards the production, deployment, use, and functionality of AI technologies.” Their account emphasizes that responsibility implicates not only technical design choices, but also the political and economic environments in which systems are embedded. Widder and Nafus (2023) similarly depict a modular “supply chain” of AI components and services based on interviews with engineers. This modularity can diffuse responsibility along the supply chain: actors assume responsibility for only the components of a system under their direct control, potentially ignoring harms elsewhere in the chain.

Other work has focused on supply chains to inform policy. Cen et al. (2023) distinguish AI supply chains from AI value chains (see also Engler and Renda 2022; Attard-Frost and Widder 2025) and emphasize the proliferation of specialized upstream providers, and highlight the implications for market power and regulation. This work motivates the need for more empirical mapping to understand how these chains operate in practice. Hopkins et al. (2025a) similarly model AI supply chains as networks, analyzing the effectiveness of upstream interventions in enforcing downstream outcomes.

6.2 Empirical Mapping of AI Ecosystems

A growing literature has sought to empirically document the structure of AI ecosystems. Bommasani et al. (2023) introduce “ecosystem graphs” for foundation models, constructing graphs that connect models, datasets, tasks, and organizations in order to surface dependencies in foundation model development and use. Laufer et al. (2025) analyze an ecosystem of two million models on the Hugging Face platform by examining interdependencies between models and components at scale. Other work has mapped particular subsectors of the AI ecosystem (e.g., open-source model ecosystems, domain-specific applications; see van der Vlist et al. 2024) or stakeholder roles in AI supply chains (Hopkins et al. 2025b).

Ecosystem-level analyses can provide valuable insight into how AI systems are built and used. However, they are often focused on a single platform, model family, or point in time. While static crawls or platform-specific metadata provide useful information about particular ecosystems, these approaches capture only a subset of the relationships that shape the AI ecosystem. Our work builds on these insights by constructing a more comprehensive dataset that dynamically tracks relationships between suppliers. Our analysis aims to make the organizational relationships that shape access to AI capabilities and influence downstream behavior cognizable. The key argument in this literature—that AI systems are produced through interdependent networks of actors and the structure of these networks bears directly on questions of governance—is our starting point. Our work builds on this approach but moves from examples to a systematic, longitudinal, empirical mapping that captures AI supply-chain relationships throughout the ecosystem.

6.3 Governance, Accountability, and Policy

A third strand of work considers the governance implications of the complex, distributed, modular AI production. Cobbe et al. (2023) discuss obstacles to accountability arising from the distributed responsibility and service-based models of AI, and opacity created by the so-called “accountability horizon,” or the limited visibility actors have into parts of the AI supply chain beyond their contractual partners. Widder and Nafus (2023) show how current responsible AI guidelines, which often assume centralized control, do not align with engineers’ actual roles in AI supply chains.

Legal scholarship has explored how supply chain structure complicates liability and compliance with copyright. For example, Lee et al. (2023) analyze generative-AI supply chains to show how upstream training data, model development, and downstream uses create complex chains of potential liability. Policy frameworks like the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act also reference supply-chain relationships. There is a growing consensus that shared responsibility and the need for transparency about upstream components and services (NIST AI, 2023).

Recent work has also highlighted the disconnect between proposals to regulate AI and the technical and institutional feasibility of those proposals. Guha et al. (2024) argue that standard regulatory approaches—licensing, registration, disclosure, and auditing—are misaligned with the technical and organizational realities of AI. One of our contributions is to ground these governance debates in empirical evidence about the AI ecosystem. Rather than assuming a particular supply chain structure, we empirically document it and show how it can shape the feasibility and efficacy of regulatory tactics.

7 Conclusion

When the barriers to entry for AI development and deployment fell, adoption grew rapidly. The result has been an increasingly complex and extensive network of organizations contributing products, services, and other assets to the AI ecosystem. That network includes not only model, data, and infrastructure providers, but also research institutions, standard-setting groups, civil society organizations, and others. Upstream in the organizational supply chain are compute and data providers; downstream are end users.

In this work, we study the organizational AI supply chain and provide a large-scale dataset that maps it. Tracing the flow of models, data, compute, infrastructure, capital, and talent through the ecosystem surfaces issues of power and control. Where the supply chain is concentrated and where chokepoints lie also indicate where risks and vulnerabilities exist in the AI ecosystem as well as where there are opportunities for transparency and regulation. By combining public documents—including news, press releases, and company blogs—with LLM extraction and network analyses, we surface contours of an ecosystem that has so far been largely obscured from systematic public view. This dataset allows for in-depth analyses of AI actor roles, concentration, dependencies, close relationships, evolving industry dynamics, uneven narratives, potential vulnerabilities, and more. One particularly important implication of this dataset is that governing AI requires governing the ecosystem and viewing it holistically. Empirical mapping of organizational relationships can provide common ground for scholars and policymakers to reason about how the AI ecosystem is organized and how it ought to be governed.

Our approach has important limitations that point toward future work. First, because the dataset is derived from public documents, it omits undisclosed relationships and over-represents high-profile firms and deals. Second, our searches are seeded through major model providers, which is only one segment of the larger supply chain. Future work should expand coverage, focus on other segments of the supply chain, and include more diverse sources of information.

Appendix B Data Filtering

This appendix details how we turn extracted relationships into the analysis graphs used in Section 5.

B.1 Base edge set

We begin with a directed edge list used by all later analyses. We keep only rows with ai_relevance ∈\in {AI_RELATIONSHIP, INVOLVES_AI_ACTOR}, a non-null relationship-classification timestamp, a non-null document_date with 2022-11-01 ≤\leq document_date << 2026-11-01 (exclusive). Undated rows and edges labeled NOT_AI_RELATED or UNCLEAR are dropped. We also drop noisy labels: actor types PERSON, NOT_AN_ACTOR, or UNKNOWN_OR_UNCLEAR on either endpoint; relationship type COMPETITION, PUBLIC_STATEMENT, NO_RELATIONSHIP, UNCLEAR, or CONTRADICTORY_INFORMATION; directionality UNCLEAR or CONTRADICTORY_INFORMATION; relationship status ENDED, NOT_APPLICABLE, UNCLEAR, or CONTRADICTORY_INFORMATION; and any edge whose AI stack layers include NOT_AI_STACK or UNKNOWN_OR_UNCLEAR. No name or edge collapse is applied yet; kept edges retain full metadata. Table 11 reports the keep / discard accounting.

B.2 Normalization

We next turn the base edge list into analysis-ready graphs by first resolving actor-name variants, then choosing how to count edges. Actor grouping proceeds in two layers. Fuzzy actor grouping applies suffix/punctuation cleanup plus fuzzy matching to the 15,406 actors in the base edge set and yields 12,907 unique actors (2,499 names remapped in the full fuzzy mapping; 1,648 multi-member clusters). Coarse actor grouping then applies a common-sense review on top (firm-family merges such as DeepMind/Alphabet/Gemini→\rightarrowGoogle, plus force-splits of known bad fuzzy clusters), changing 5,013 names relative to the fuzzy mapping and bringing the actor set to 9,699 before the low-frequency filter. Table 12 summarizes these layers.

Edge normalization then chooses how to count ties. Raw (multiplicity) keeps one edge per extracted relationship (reporting intensity). Indicator collapses rows that share the same endpoints, directionality, relationship type, and calendar period—AI stack layer is omitted from the key—so each distinct typed tie in that period counts once; the period may be month or week. For SYMMETRIC/UNCLEAR edges, endpoint order does not matter. Rows labeled ACTOR_1_TO_ACTOR_2 or ACTOR_2_TO_ACTOR_1 in gsearch_relationship_results are stored as DIRECTIONAL; backward rows have the endpoints swapped so actor1 is the source, and that order is kept after name mapping.

Low-frequency actor filter. After name mapping, we count multiplicity relationships per canonical actor across the corpus and drop any actor with fewer than three such relationships. We then induce the edge set—keeping an edge only if both endpoints meet the threshold—and rebuild the indicator graphs from the filtered multiplicity. Actors that meet the threshold but lose all neighbors under induction are also removed. This step drops sparsely attested name strings from the analysis graphs.

We write Gg,rawG^{g,\mathrm{raw}} for a raw graph under actor grouping g∈{fuzzy,coarse}g\in\{\mathrm{fuzzy},\mathrm{coarse}\}, and Gt,g,indicatorG^{t,g,\mathrm{indicator}} when the indicator uses time grain t∈{month,week}t\in\{\mathrm{month},\mathrm{week}\}. Crossing the two groupings with raw and the two indicator grains gives six graphs after this filter. Table 13 lists nodes and edges for each. Downstream findings use Gmonth,coarse,indicatorG^{\mathrm{month},\mathrm{coarse},\mathrm{indicator}} unless noted.

Actor-type edge counts include an edge if either endpoint has that type.

Appendix F Additional Results for Section 4.4

Figure 28 ranks publishers by volume. Yahoo Finance alone accounts for about 21% of multiplicity edges, followed by TechCrunch (17%) and VentureBeat (7.5%). Across 2,561 publishers, the top 10% contribute about 81% of edges.

Figure 29 shows the mean number of distinct documents per collapsed tie for each seed organization. Relationships that share the same endpoints, type, directionality, and calendar month form one tie. A tie is included for an organization when that organization is an endpoint. Names are the normalized actor names, so DeepMind and Google AI are Google, and Microsoft AI is Microsoft. 01.AI, Contextual AI, and Reka AI average more than 2.5 documents per tie. Among organizations that appear in thousands of ties, OpenAI is highest, about 1.9.

Figure 30 reports the largest number of distinct documents on any one collapsed tie for each seed organization. A tie is included for an organization when that organization is an endpoint. OpenAI, Microsoft, and Hugging Face reach 35 documents (OpenAI and Microsoft on a shared April 2026 partnership tie; OpenAI and Hugging Face on a shared July 2026 incident tie). Anthropic, NVIDIA, and xAI reach 31.

Figure 31 breaks the same monthly ties out by relationship type for the four outlets that carry the most of them. Each tie is assigned to the publisher that accounts for the most of its extracted rows. Yahoo’s regional finance sites are counted together. Yahoo is the largest source of partnership, provision, and ownership ties. TechCrunch is the largest source of investment ties, with about 2,600 such ties against about 1,600 from Yahoo. CNBC appears in every major type, at much lower volume.

Appendix G Dataset Documentation

The public Hugging Face release (sarahcen/ai-supply-chain) is a parquet table of AI-related relationship rows. Table 1 gives an abbreviated overview in the main text; Table 16 lists every published column with full categorical value sets. The release includes ai_relevance, relationship_status, and ai_stack_layers. Directed rows are stored as ACTOR_1_TO_ACTOR_2 or ACTOR_2_TO_ACTOR_1. The analysis graphs rewrite both labels to DIRECTIONAL and, for the second label, swap the endpoints so actor 1 is the source. Published rows keep only AI_RELATIONSHIP and INVOLVES_AI_ACTOR, and drop rows whose relationship type, status, or directionality is CONTRADICTORY_INFORMATION.
